subChunks.title: Research Ethics: Principles, Regulation & Hard Cases
subChunks.hookHtml: In 1971, Philip Zimbardo began what he later described as 'the most dramatic yet least expected result' of his career as a psychologist. Twenty-four male Stanford students were randomly assigned to play the roles of 'prisoners' or 'guards' in a simulated prison in the basement of Stanford's psychology department. What happened over the next six days became one of the most cited — and most contested — studies in psychology's history. Guards became increasingly abusive; prisoners broke down and begged to be released; Zimbardo himself, playing the role of 'prison superintendent', became so absorbed in the situation that he failed to stop the study even as participants showed distress. He ended it on day six following the intervention of a graduate student — Christina Maslach — who refused to accept what was happening as 'just research.' The Stanford Prison Experiment raised foundational questions about research ethics that reverberate to this day: When does the scientific value of knowledge justify exposing participants to psychological harm? Who decides what counts as justified risk? Can researchers who are immersed in their own studies be trusted to monitor participant welfare? And what happens to scientific fields when landmark studies that shaped textbooks and theories turn out to have methodological and ethical problems more serious than originally acknowledged? Research ethics is not a box-ticking compliance exercise. It is the set of principles, practices, and institutional structures that determine whether psychology can be trusted — by the public, by participants, and by the scientists who conduct it.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Historical Background: From Nuremberg to BPS

Modern research ethics developed in response to documented abuses:

  • Nazi medical experiments: The Nuremberg Code (1947) established foundational principles including voluntary consent, proportionate risk, freedom to withdraw, and qualified researchers.
  • Tuskegee Syphilis Study (1932–1972): 399 Black men with syphilis were observed without treatment even after penicillin became available — producing the Belmont Report (1979) and the principles of respect for persons, beneficence, and justice.
  • Milgram obedience experiments (1963): Participants believed they were administering potentially lethal electric shocks to a learner. No physical harm occurred, but psychological distress was significant and the study raised questions about deception, debriefing, and long-term effects of participation.
  • Willowbrook hepatitis studies (1956–1970): Intellectually disabled children were deliberately infected with hepatitis at Willowbrook State School, raising issues of consent by proxy and institutional exploitation of vulnerable populations.

These abuses drove the development of institutional review boards (IRBs) in the US and ethics committees in the UK, professional codes (APA, BPS), and regulatory frameworks governing research with human participants.

Core Principles of Research Ethics

The BPS Code of Human Research Ethics (2021) is organised around four principles:

Respect for autonomy and dignity: Participants must give informed consent — understanding the purpose, procedures, risks, and their right to withdraw without penalty. Deception is only permissible where: the research question cannot be addressed without it; the deception is not severely distressing; full debriefing is provided. The right to withdraw includes the right to withdraw data after participation.

Scientific value: Research should have scientific merit proportionate to any risks or burdens placed on participants. The obligation to produce knowledge of value (not just avoid harm) is itself an ethical requirement.

Social responsibility: Research should benefit individuals and society. Psychologists have responsibilities to the wider public as well as to participants — this includes obligations around dissemination, public communication, and avoiding harm to third parties.

Maximising benefit and minimising harm: Risk-benefit analysis — are the potential benefits (to knowledge, to society, to future participants) proportionate to the risks (to participants, to groups represented, to public trust)?

Specific Ethical Issues in Psychological Research

Informed consent: Valid consent requires: capacity (the ability to understand and use information), information (adequate disclosure), voluntariness (no coercion or undue influence). Special considerations for: children (assent + parental consent, but Gillick competence applies); people with intellectual disability; prisoners and other institutionalised populations (where voluntariness is compromised by power differentials).

Deception and debriefing: Some of the most influential social psychology studies used deception (Milgram, Asch, Zimbardo). The contemporary ethics framework permits deception only where it is methodologically necessary, not severely distressing, and followed by thorough debriefing that restores full understanding. Retrospective consent after debriefing is acceptable in some cases. Active deception (telling participants something false) is subject to stricter scrutiny than passive deception (not revealing full purpose).

Confidentiality and data protection: Participants have the right to expect that identifying information will not be disclosed without consent. Limits: safeguarding obligations; legal requirements; data governance under UK GDPR.

Internet research: Online data collection raises novel ethical questions: what counts as 'public' data (tweets, forum posts)? Can participants in online communities meaningfully consent when data are scraped at scale? When is anonymisation sufficient?

Research with vulnerable populations: Extra protections required for: children, people with intellectual disability, people with mental illness, prisoners, people in acute distress. 'Double effect' situations where participation in research may be the only route to accessing services (e.g., clinical trials) create coercive pressure that requires careful management.

Open Science and Research Integrity

The replication crisis (see psy-lea-1) has made research integrity a front-and-centre ethical issue. Questionable research practices (QRPs) — p-hacking, selective outcome reporting, HARKing (hypothesising after results known), salami-slicing, undisclosed flexibility in analysis — produce a misleading scientific literature. These are not merely methodological failures: they are ethical violations of the principles of truthfulness and social responsibility. Open science practices (pre-registration, data sharing, open materials, registered reports) are ethical practices as well as methodological improvements.

storyBeats.text: Dr. Chen asks: 'If you could run the Milgram study knowing what we know now — and you could design it so participants understood it was all staged from the beginning — what would you learn? And would that knowledge be worth the deception in the original design?' The room debates.

storyBeats.speaker: Dr. Miriam Chen
storyBeats.text: The Milgram studies produced knowledge that is still important — about authority, obedience, situational factors in moral behaviour. But the means by which that knowledge was obtained are now considered ethically unacceptable, and not only because of the distress experienced in the moment. Milgram's participants were told, retrospectively, that they had demonstrated a capacity for cruelty that they did not know they had. The debriefing did not fully undo that. Some of them carried that knowledge for the rest of their lives. The research question 'what would you do?' had an answer that the participants did not want.

storyBeats.speaker: The Stanford Prison Experiment revisited
storyBeats.text: For decades, the Stanford Prison Experiment was taught as demonstrating the power of situational factors to produce brutal behaviour. In 2019, journalist Ben Blum obtained recordings of Zimbardo coaching guards on how to behave and of guards discussing performing their roles. Subsequent investigation found that many guard behaviours were performative rather than genuinely spontaneous; that prisoners who 'broke down' may have been playing a role they understood was expected; and that Zimbardo's immersion in the study superintendent role genuinely compromised his ethical oversight. The study's findings — once used to explain Abu Ghraib — are now methodologically and ethically contested. This is not merely a historical lesson: it shows how institutional and financial pressures, authority gradients, and researcher investment in outcomes can compromise ethical oversight in research settings.

storyBeats.speaker: Dr. Miriam Chen
storyBeats.text: Questionable research practices are not victimless. When a researcher p-hacks a finding into significance and publishes it, clinicians may adopt an ineffective treatment. When a drug company selectively reports positive trials, patients receive medications whose benefits they have been systematically misled about. When a psychologist HARKs their hypothesis, other researchers waste years and resources trying to build on a finding that never existed. Research integrity is an ethical obligation, not just a methodological aspiration — and the culture of publish-or-perish that incentivises these practices is itself an ethical problem that the field must address.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
A research team proposes a study examining whether childhood exposure to domestic violence predicts adult attachment style. They plan to recruit 200 adults from a domestic violence charity's database, administer a retrospective childhood experiences questionnaire (asking detailed questions about violence witnessed in the home), and an adult attachment measure. The charity has agreed to send recruitment emails to their client database. The team notes that some of the charity's clients are currently in crisis or actively seeking support.

  1. Identify three specific ethical issues with this research design and explain the principle violated by each.
  2. The team argues that the research has high scientific value because understanding this relationship could help design better interventions. How should this scientific value claim be weighed against the identified risks?
  3. Propose two specific modifications to the research design that would address the most serious ethical concerns while preserving the scientific value of the study.
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
1. Three ethical issues: (a) Voluntary participation / undue influence: Recruiting from a domestic violence charity's active client database creates a potentially coercive recruitment context. Clients may feel obligated to participate to maintain a positive relationship with the charity that is supporting them; they may fear that non-participation could affect their access to services; or staff recruitment may implicitly communicate an expectation of participation. This violates the principle of voluntariness — valid consent requires the absence of undue influence. Clients in crisis are particularly vulnerable to this dynamic. (b) Consent capacity and protection of vulnerable participants: The researchers acknowledge some clients are 'currently in crisis or actively seeking support.' People in acute crisis may have temporarily reduced capacity to make fully reflective decisions about research participation; their ability to weigh risks and benefits, and to exercise the right to withdraw without pressure, may be compromised. The BPS Code requires extra protection for people in acute distress — including additional safeguards for consent, monitoring during participation, and available support. (c) Potential psychological harm from retrospective trauma recall: Detailed retrospective questioning about childhood domestic violence exposure is likely to activate traumatic memories in participants who have experienced this adversity. This is not a reason to not conduct the research, but it creates obligations: risk of significant distress must be assessed; support resources must be immediately available; the consent process must clearly explain what questions will be asked; and participants should be debriefed with clear signposting to support if distress is activated.

2. Weighing scientific value against risk: The scientific value claim is legitimate — understanding the relationship between childhood domestic violence exposure and adult attachment has clear therapeutic implications for intervention design and could benefit future clients. However, scientific value does not automatically override risk, particularly for vulnerable populations. The ethical framework requires the potential benefits to be proportionate to the burdens placed on participants, and extra weight should be given to vulnerability. In this case: (a) the same research question could potentially be addressed with lower-risk participant recruitment (e.g., general population recruitment with retrospective exposure questions, rather than targeting an active crisis service client base); (b) the scientific value of using an active client database specifically (rather than alternative recruitment) needs justification — is there a specific scientific reason why this client population is essential, rather than adults with childhood DV exposure recruited more broadly? If not, the scientific value does not justify the specific risks of crisis-service recruitment. The principle of scientific value also requires the research to be methodologically sound — retrospective self-report of childhood experiences has significant reliability limitations (recall bias, reinterpretation through adult frameworks) that should be acknowledged.

3. Two design modifications: (a) Change recruitment to adults who have completed support (not currently in crisis): Rather than recruiting from active clients, recruit from individuals who engaged with the charity at least 6 months ago and have completed their active support period. This substantially reduces the coercive recruitment context and the vulnerability concern while retaining access to a relevant population. The charity should communicate clearly in recruitment materials that participation is entirely voluntary and unconnected to any ongoing or future services. (b) Provide accessible psychological support and safeguarding protocol: Before data collection, implement: (i) a brief wellbeing screening question at the start of the questionnaire allowing participants to indicate current high distress and exit with immediate support information; (ii) a clear, prominent debrief page following the retrospective trauma questions providing immediate access to the charity's support line, national helplines, and crisis resources; and (iii) a researcher contact protocol for participants who disclose current crisis or acute suicidal ideation. These measures address the harm minimisation obligation without preventing research from proceeding.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: The open science movement argues that practices like pre-registration, data sharing, and open materials are not merely methodological improvements but ethical obligations — that a researcher who p-hacks or selectively reports outcomes commits an ethical violation, not just a methodological error. Critically evaluate this argument. Aim for 200–250 words.
subChunks.modelAnswer:
The argument that questionable research practices are ethical violations, not merely methodological errors, has substantial force. The distinction between 'methodological error' and 'ethical violation' rests on the claim that the latter involves harm to others. Questionable research practices do produce harm:

Clinicians who adopt interventions whose efficacy evidence was produced through p-hacking or selective outcome reporting may offer patients ineffective or harmful treatments. The antidepressant publication bias case demonstrates this at scale: patients received medications whose published efficacy overstated their true effects because negative trials were not published. These are not victimless errors — they affect real patients.

Funding bodies and other researchers who invest resources building on non-replicable findings incur real costs that would not exist if the underlying findings had been honestly reported. Replication failures consume enormous research resources that could have been directed elsewhere.

The research community and public are deceived when researchers present conclusions as supported by evidence that selective reporting has manufactured. This violates the BPS principle of truthfulness and social responsibility.

However, the argument risks overcriminalising exploratory research practices that are not inherently dishonest. Exploratory analysis — running multiple analyses, testing different specifications — is legitimate provided it is transparent and clearly labelled. The ethical violation lies in presenting exploratory findings as confirmatory, not in the exploration itself.

The most defensible position: deliberate, undisclosed p-hacking and selective outcome reporting are ethical violations. Pre-registration, data sharing, and transparent reporting are ethical obligations proportionate to the potential harms of their absence. Inadvertent QRPs require education and structural reform, not primarily moral condemnation.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a 16-year-old why Milgram's famous obedience experiments — which showed most people will give electric shocks if told to by an authority figure — would not be allowed today, even though the results were important.

rabbitHoleTerms.description: The 1979 US report establishing three foundational principles for research ethics: respect for persons (autonomy and protection of those with diminished autonomy), beneficence (maximise benefits and minimise harm), and justice (fair distribution of research burdens and benefits). Foundational for US IRB regulations.

A process (not a single document) by which research participants make a fully informed, voluntary decision to participate. Three components: capacity (ability to understand and use information), adequate information disclosure, and voluntariness (no coercion or undue influence). Adapted for children, people with intellectual disability, and others with reduced decision-making capacity.

Hypothesising After Results Known — presenting post-hoc hypotheses (generated after seeing data) as if they were a priori predictions. A questionable research practice that inflates false positive rates and misleads the literature; considered an ethical as well as methodological violation under open science norms.

A publication format in which the introduction and methods of a study are peer-reviewed and accepted before data collection — journals commit to publishing the results regardless of findings. Directly addresses publication bias and selective outcome reporting by decoupling publication from results.

questions.questionHtml: What are the three foundational principles of research ethics established by the Belmont Report (1979)?
options: Respect for persons, beneficence, and justice
Informed consent, minimal harm, and scientific value
questions.correctAnswer: Respect for persons, beneficence, and justice
questions.explanationHtml: The Belmont Report, produced in response to the Tuskegee Syphilis Study and other research abuses, established three foundational principles: (1) Respect for persons — treating individuals as autonomous agents and protecting those with diminished autonomy; operationalised as informed consent; (2) Beneficence — obligations to maximise benefits and minimise harms; not just 'do no harm' but actively promote wellbeing; (3) Justice — fair distribution of the benefits and burdens of research; those who bear research burdens (participants) should benefit, and vulnerable populations should not be exploited for research benefiting others. These principles remain foundational for research ethics frameworks worldwide, including the BPS Code, Declaration of Helsinki, and US IRB regulations.

questions.questionHtml: True or False: Research using deception is absolutely prohibited under the BPS Code of Human Research Ethics.
questions.explanationHtml: False. Deception is permitted under the BPS Code under specific conditions — it is not absolutely prohibited. The conditions for permissible deception include: the research question cannot be adequately addressed without deception; the deception does not involve severe distress or lasting harm; participants are fully debriefed as soon as reasonably possible after participation; and retrospective consent is obtained where appropriate. The rationale is that absolute prohibition of deception would eliminate research into phenomena that cannot be studied when participants know the true purpose (e.g., demand characteristics, social desirability). Active deception (telling participants something false) is subject to stricter scrutiny than passive deception (not fully disclosing the purpose). The key is proportionality — the scientific value of the knowledge justifies the degree of deception involved, and robust debriefing is essential.

questions.questionHtml: A researcher selects the statistical analysis approach for their data after examining several alternatives and finding that only one produces a significant result. They report only this analysis. Which ethical principle have they most clearly violated?
options: Informed consent — participants were not told about the multiple analyses
Scientific value — the research no longer has scientific merit
Truthfulness and social responsibility — selective reporting misrepresents the evidence to the scientific community and potential users of the research
Confidentiality — participant data has been shared inappropriately
questions.correctAnswer: Truthfulness and social responsibility — selective reporting misrepresents the evidence to the scientific community and potential users of the research
questions.explanationHtml: The practice described is p-hacking or selective outcome reporting — a questionable research practice that produces false positive findings by exploiting analytical flexibility. The most directly violated ethical principle is truthfulness: the researcher is presenting a result as if it were a pre-specified analysis when it was selected post-hoc because it produced the desired result — this is a form of deception of the scientific community. Social responsibility is also violated: clinicians and practitioners who use the published finding to guide practice may adopt an ineffective intervention; funding bodies and other researchers who invest resources building on the finding waste resources that could have been directed elsewhere. The BPS Code's principle of social responsibility includes obligations to produce honest, accurate representations of findings. This is an ethical violation — not merely a methodological error — because it involves deliberate misrepresentation with potential real-world harm.
